title: Garhwal by season and altitude
meta_description: When to visit Garhwal: month by month weather, shrine opening and closing, monsoon risk, snow at Auli and Chopta, and how to handle altitude above 3,000 m.
summary: The best months for Garhwal's high valleys are May–June and mid-September to October, when the Char Dham shrines are open and roads are dry. July and August bring flowers and landslides. Winter is for Rishikesh, Mussoorie, Auli and Chopta. Four shrines sit above 3,000 m, so plan sleeping heights with care.

sections.heading: Two seasons, month by month
paras: Garhwal runs from 340 m at Rishikesh to the snow peaks above 7,000 m on the Tibet border, so asking when to visit is really asking where. In practice the region has two travel seasons. The yatra season runs from the opening of the shrines in late April or May until they close around Diwali and in November, with a monsoon gap in the middle. The winter season, from December to March, belongs to the lower hills, the ski slope at Auli and snow walks around Chopta.

The rule we give most travellers is simple. Go high in May and June or from mid-September to October. Go low, or to Auli, from December to March. In July and August, go only for the Valley of Flowers, and keep spare days.
The table gives our rating and typical temperatures. Ratings are for the region as a whole; Rishikesh is at its best in winter, when the high valleys are closed.

sections.heading: Spring and early summer: April to June
paras: The yatra year begins with the kapat opening. Yamunotri and Gangotri open on Akshaya Tritiya, usually in late April or early May. The Kedarnath date is announced at Ukhimath on Mahashivratri and the Badrinath date at the Narendra Nagar palace on Basant Panchami; both usually fall between late April and mid-May. The first weeks are the most crowded of the year, with long queues and full hotels, and snow can still line the Kedarnath path.

By late May the high roads are clear, rhododendrons have given way to green, and the bugyals above Chopta and Auli begin to turn. June is hot in Rishikesh, often 38 °C, and busy everywhere because of school holidays. The Valley of Flowers opens on 1 June, with snow bridges and early blooms. Pre-monsoon showers start in the second half of June; finish high treks by then if you want dry trails.

sections.heading: Monsoon: July and August
paras: The southwest monsoon reaches Garhwal in late June and stays until mid-September. It is the season of the Valley of Flowers, at its peak from mid-July to mid-August, and of Hemkund Sahib's busiest pilgrim weeks. It is also the season of landslides, washed-out bridges and roads closed for hours or days. The Kedarnath disaster of June 2013 and the Dharali flash flood near Harsil in August 2025 both happened in monsoon.
If you travel now, follow a few rules:
list: Check IMD and district alerts every evening and follow police and SDRF instructions on the road.
Never drive hill roads after dark in rain, and do not cross streams in spate on foot.
Keep at least two spare days between the mountains and your train or flight.
Carry a waterproof jacket, pack cover and quick-dry clothes; cotton never dries.
Rafting on the Ganga is closed from July to mid-September.

sections.heading: Autumn and winter: September to March
paras: From mid-September the rain stops, the air clears and the yatra resumes with smaller crowds. October is our favourite month: views from Chandrashila and Auli are at their sharpest, apples hang in Harsil, and hotel rates on the yatra road are lower. Nights at Kedarnath and Badrinath fall below freezing. The shrines close around Diwali: Gangotri and Yamunotri around the festival, Kedarnath on Bhai Dooj, and Badrinath a couple of weeks later. Each deity moves to its winter seat at Mukhba, Kharsali, Ukhimath, and Pandukeshwar and Jyotirmath.

December to March is the low-hills season. Rishikesh is mild and clear, Mussoorie gets occasional snow, and Auli runs ski courses when snow allows, usually January to March. Chopta often gets snow from January, and the road above Duggalbitta may close; Tungnath is then a winter walk with microspikes and a local guide. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Festivals and crowds through the year
paras: Crowds in Garhwal follow the religious calendar and the school calendar more than the weather. The first week after each shrine opens is the busiest of the year, and Char Dham registration has at times been capped per day at each temple to manage the numbers. The Hindi-belt summer holidays, from late May to June, then fill Mussoorie, Rishikesh and every yatra town. Ganga Dussehra, in late May or June, brings lakhs of bathers to Haridwar and large crowds to Rishikesh.

Early March is quieter in the hills but busy in Rishikesh, where Parmarth Niketan holds its International Yoga Festival in the first week. Weekends in October and the Christmas to New Year week fill Mussoorie. The quietest high-valley weeks are usually the last two of September and the second half of October, after the monsoon and before the closing ceremonies. If you want to see a doli procession without the crowd at the shrine, wait for it at Ukhimath or Mukhba when the deities come down for winter.

sections.heading: What to pack by season
paras: Layers matter more than any single heavy coat, because a day can start at 30 °C in Rishikesh and end near freezing at Badrinath. Pack for the highest place you will sleep, not the place you start.
list: May–June: sun hat, sunscreen and light cottons for the plains; fleece, down jacket, cap and gloves for nights above 3,000 m.
July–August: waterproof jacket and trousers, pack cover, quick-dry clothes, sandals for wet days and a headlamp for power cuts.
September–October: warm down jacket, thermals and gloves for nights at the shrines; light layers for the days.
December–March: thermals, insulated jacket, waterproof boots, microspikes for Chopta and Tungnath, and sunglasses for snow.
All year: a refillable steel bottle, basic medicines, any prescriptions and a printed copy of your registration and bookings.

sections.heading: Altitude: what changes above 3,000 m
paras: Four of Garhwal's most visited places are above 3,000 m: Kedarnath at 3,583 m, Badrinath at about 3,300 m, Yamunotri at about 3,293 m and Gangotri at about 3,100 m. Ghangaria is at 3,049 m, and Hemkund Sahib and Chandrashila top 4,000 m. Many visitors reach these heights within a day or two of leaving the plains, which is how altitude sickness happens.

Acute mountain sickness shows as headache, nausea, poor sleep, dizziness and unusual tiredness. It is common and usually mild if you slow down, but it can become serious. The yatra administration runs health screening points and medical posts on the main routes, and has advised older pilgrims and those with heart or lung conditions to get a check-up before travel. Talk to your doctor before you go, especially about any medicines for altitude.
list: Sleep low before going high: Guptkashi or Sitapur before Kedarnath, Harsil before Gangotri, Joshimath before Badrinath.
Walk slowly, drink water often and avoid alcohol for the first nights at height.
A helicopter does not prevent altitude sickness; it gets you high faster, so rest on arrival.
If symptoms get worse, go down; descent of even 500 m helps.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Garhwal?
faqs.a: May–June and mid-September to October for the high valleys and Char Dham, when roads are dry and shrines open. December to March suits Rishikesh, Mussoorie and Auli. July and August are for the Valley of Flowers only, with spare days.

faqs.q: When do the Char Dham temples open and close?
faqs.a: Yamunotri and Gangotri open on Akshaya Tritiya in late April or May. Kedarnath and Badrinath open on dates announced in February or March. All close around Diwali, Badrinath last in November. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to travel to Garhwal in monsoon?
faqs.a: It is possible but risky. Landslides close roads for hours or days, and flash floods have hit the region. Follow official alerts, avoid driving after dark, keep two spare days and avoid July if you can.
Snow usually settles from late December or January to March, and ski courses run in that window when cover is good. Snowfall varies a lot by year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Valley of Flowers in full bloom?
faqs.a: From mid-July to mid-August most species flower. The park is usually open from 1 June to 31 October, with fewer flowers in June and September.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness at Kedarnath?
faqs.a: Many people feel mild symptoms like headache or breathlessness at 3,583 m, especially after a fast ascent by helicopter. Sleep low the night before, walk slowly, drink water and come down if symptoms worsen. Talk to your doctor first.

faqs.q: Is October too cold for Kedarnath and Badrinath?
faqs.a: Days are clear and pleasant, around 10–14 °C, but nights drop below freezing. A down jacket, thermal layers, gloves and a cap are enough for most people.

faqs.q: Can I visit Chopta and Tungnath in winter?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days, but snow may close the road above Duggalbitta and the temple is closed. Walk with microspikes and a local guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Rishikesh too hot in summer?
faqs.a: May and June often reach 35–39 °C by day. Mornings and evenings by the river are fine. For comfort, visit from October to April.
